---
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Let $x \in G$ and $H \leqslant G$.
	The {\itshape relative order} of $x$ with respect to $H$ is
	$$ o_H(x) \> := \> | \langle x \rangle : \langle x \rangle \cap H | . $$
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lemRelOrd}
	 Let $n \geq 1$.
	Then $x^n \in H$ if and only if $o_H(x)$ is finite and divides $n$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{corCrit}
	$x^{|G:H|} \in H$ if and only if $|H \langle x \rangle:H|$ divides $|G:H|$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{propSubn}
	Let $H \lhd \lhd \> G$. Then $|HK:K|$ divides $|G:K|$ for every $K \leqslant_f G$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thSubn2}
	Let $H \leqslant_f G$. Then $H \lhd \lhd \> G$ if and only if $|HK:H|$ divides $|G:H|$ for every $K \leqslant G$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
A subgroup $H \leqslant_f G$ is {\itshape exponential} if $x^{|G:H|} \in H$ for every $x \in G$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thSExp}
	If $G$ is any group, then $S(G) = \cap_{N \lhd_f G} F_N(G)$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $ord_H(x) := \min \{ n \geq 1: x^n \in H \}$.
	We first notice that $o_H(x)=ord_H(x)$.
	Indeed, from the definitions we have $o_H(x)=o_{H \cap \langle x \rangle}(x)$ and $ord_H(x)=ord_{H \cap \langle x \rangle}(x)$.
	The fact that $o_{H \cap \langle x \rangle}(x) = ord_{H \cap \langle x \rangle}(x)$
	is a simple exercise.
	Now, the ``if'' part of the statement is trivial.
	On the other hand, if $x^n \in H$ for some $n \geq 1$, then clearly $ord_H(x) < \infty$. 
	Let $n = q \cdot ord_H(x) + r$ with $r,q \geq 0$ and $r<ord_H(x)$. 
	Since $H$ is a subgroup, the fact that $x^n = x^{q \cdot ord_H(x)} x^r \in H$ implies that $x^r \in H$,
	which in turn means $r=0$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lemTool}
	Let $H \lhd M \leqslant G$, and let $K \leqslant_f G$. Then $|HK:K|$ divides $|MK:K|$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
We have to prove that the ratio
	$$ \frac{|MK:K|}{|HK:K|} = \frac{|M:M \cap K|}{|H:H \cap K|} $$ 
	is an integer.
	Now $H \lhd M$ implies that $H(M \cap K)$ is a subgroup of $M$, and so we can write
	  \begin{align*}
|M:M \cap K|  & \> = \> 
|M:H(M \cap K)| |H(M \cap K):M \cap K| \\ & \> = \> 
 |M:H(M \cap K)| |H:H \cap K|  .
\end{align*}
	In particular, the original ratio equals $|M:H(M \cap K)|$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lemTool2}
	Let $H \leqslant_f M \leqslant_f G$, and let $K \leqslant G$. Then $\frac{|HK:H|}{|MK:M|}=|M \cap K:H \cap K|$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
We have
	\begin{align*}
	\frac{|HK:H|}{|MK:M|}  & \> = \> 
	\frac{|K:H \cap K|}{|K:M \cap K|}  \\ & \> = \> 
	\frac{|K:M \cap K| |M \cap K:H \cap K|}{|K:M \cap K|}  \\ & \> = \> 
	 |M \cap K:H \cap K| . \qedhere
	\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a finite group, $H \leqslant G$, and let $p$ be a prime.
	Then $H$ is {\itshape $p$-subnormal} in $G$ if $H \cap P$ is a $p$-Sylow of $H$ for every $p$-Sylow $P$ of $G$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lemPSubNChar}
	A subgroup $H$ is $p$-subnormal if and only if $|HP|$ divides $|G|$ for every $p$-Sylow $P \leqslant G$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
We have that $H \cap P$ is a $p$-Sylow of $H$ if and only if $|H:H \cap P|=|HP:P|$ is not divisible by $p$.
	Since $|H:H \cap P|$ is a divisor of $|G|$, the last condition is equivalent to $|HP:P|$ dividing $|G:P|$, i.e. $|HP| \mid |G|$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thKW}
	If $|HP|$ divides $|G|$ for every Sylow subgroup $P \leqslant G$, then $H \lhd \lhd \> G$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lemKleidNilp}
	Let $H \leqslant G$ be a nilpotent subgroup of the finite group $G$.
	If $|HP|$ divides $|G|$ for every Sylow subgroup $P \leqslant G$, then $H \lhd \lhd \> G$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Suppose that $H$ is not subnormal, and in particular $H \nleqslant F(G)$.
	So there exists a $p$-element $x$ such that $x \in H \setminus F(G)$.
	Since $x \notin O_p(G)$, there exists a $p$-Sylow $P$ of $G$ such that $x \notin P$.
	By hypothesis $H \cap P$ is a $p$-Sylow of $H$ and, since $H$ is nilpotent, $H \cap P$ contains all the $p$-elements of $H$.
	This contradicts the fact that $x \notin P$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a finite group and $H \leqslant G$.
	If $|HP|$ divides $|G|$ for every Sylow $P \leqslant G$,
	then $|HK|$ divides $|G|$ for every $K \leqslant G$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let $K \leqslant G$. We have to show that $|HK:K|=|H:H \cap K|$ divides $|G:K|$.
	Let $p^\alpha$ be a prime power that divides $|H:H \cap K|$.
	Since $p^\alpha$ is arbitrary, it is sufficient to prove that $p^\alpha \mid |G:K|$.
	Let $P_0 \leqslant K$ be a $p$-Sylow of $K$, and let $P \leqslant G$ be a $p$-Sylow of $G$ such that $P \cap K=P_0$.
	Of course, $p^\alpha \mid |H:H \cap P_0|$.
	By hypothesis $|H:H \cap P|=|HP : P|$ divides $|G:P|$, and so is not divisible by $p$.
	Therefore, $p^\alpha \mid |H \cap P:H \cap P_0|$.
	Now $|H \cap P:H \cap P_0|=|(H \cap P)P_0:P_0|$,
	and this divides $|P:P_0|$ because $P$ is a $p$-group.
	So $p^\alpha \mid |P:P_0|$, and then of course $p^\alpha \mid |G:P_0|$.
	Since $p \nmid |K:P_0|$, we obtain $p^\alpha \mid |G:K|$ as desired.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lemExpQuot}
 Let $N \lhd G$, and $N \leqslant H \leqslant G$. Then $H \leqslant_{exp} G$ if and only if $H/N \leqslant_{exp} G/N$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let $x \in G$ and $H \leqslant_{exp} G$. Then $(Nx)^{|G/N:H/N|}=Nx^{|G:H|} \in H/N$ and so $H/N \leqslant_{exp} G/N$.
 If $H/N \leqslant_{exp} G/N$, then $Nx^{|G:H|} = (Nx)^{|G/N:H/N|} \in H$, and so $x^{|G:H|} \in H$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Every finite group of order other than a prime has a non-trivial exponential subgroup:
	if $\exp(G)<|G|$, then it is sufficient to take any subgroup whose order divides $|G|/\exp(G)$.
	Otherwise, all the Sylow subgroups of $G$ are cyclic,
	and it is well known that $G$ is solvable.
	In particular, $G$ has a non-trivial normal subgroup, which is certainly exponential.\\
	We notice a difference with the stronger condition that $HK$ is a subgroup for every $K$
	i.e. $H$ is a {\itshape permutable} subgroup.
	Indeed, it is easy to prove that if $HC$ is a subgroup for every cyclic $C \leqslant G$, 
	 then $HK$ is a subgroup for every $K \leqslant G$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lemNew}
	Let $H \leqslant G$ have a trivial characteristic core.
	Then $H \leqslant_{exp} G$ if and only if $|G:H|$ is a multiple of the exponent of $G$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let $n=|G:H|$.
	By the exponentiality of $H$ we have $G^n \leqslant H$.
	Since $G^n$ is a characteristic subgroup of $G$ contained in $H$, we obtain $G^n=1$.
	But this means exactly that $n$ is a multiple of $\exp(G)$.
	The converse is trivial.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
Let $H \leqslant G$ be a Hall subgroup. If $H \leqslant_{exp} G$, then $H \lhd G$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Suppose that $H$ is not normal, and let $N \lhd G$ be the normal core of $H$.
	Since $H/N$ is a Hall subgroup of $G/N$, by induction and Lemma \ref{lemExpQuot}, we can assume that $H$ is core-free.
	Now $\exp(G)$ captures every prime dividing $|G|$, and so the contradiction is given by Lemma \ref{lemNew}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{corMaxExp}
	Let $M \leqslant G$ be a maximal subgroup of the solvable group $G$. If $M \leqslant_{exp} G$, then $M \lhd G$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Suppose that $M$ is not normal, and let $N \lhd G$ be the normal core of $M$.
	Since $M/N$ is a maximal subgroup of $G/N$, by induction and Lemma \ref{lemExpQuot}, we can assume that $M$ is core-free.
	Now $|G:M|=q^\alpha$ for some prime power $q^\alpha$.
	If $G$ is a $q$-group we are done. Otherwise, the contradiction is given by Lemma \ref{lemNew}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
The following are true:
\begin{itemize}
\item If $H \leqslant_{exp} M \leqslant_{exp} G$, then $H \leqslant_{exp} G$;
\item The intersection of exponential subgroups is exponential.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $x \in G$. Since $M \leqslant_{exp} G$, we have $m=x^{|G:M|} \in M$.
Then $x^{|G:H|}=m^{|M:H|} \in H$.
To prove the second statement, it is sufficient to notice that $|G:H \cap K|$ is a multiple of both $|G:H|$ and $|G:K|$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{propFitting}
	If $G$ is finite, then $S(G)=F(G)$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let $x \in G$. Then $x \in S(G)$ if and only if $|H \langle x \rangle|$ divides $|G|$ for every $H \leqslant G$.
	From Proposition \ref{propSubn} and Lemma \ref{lemKleidNilp}, this is equivalent to $\langle x \rangle \lhd \lhd \> G$, i.e. $x \in F(G)$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lemReductionRF}
	Let $N \lhd G$.
	Then $S(G/N) = \{ Nx : x^{|G:H|} \in H \mbox{ for every } N \leqslant H \leqslant_f G \}$.
	In particular, $S(G/R(G)) = S(G)/R(G)$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Let $x \in G$ and $N \leqslant H \leqslant_f G$.
	The equality $(Nx)^{|G:H|} = Nx^{|G:H|}$ implies that $Nx \in H/N$ if and only if $x^{|G:H|} \in H$,
	and the first part follows because $H$ is arbitrary.
	The second part follows because $R(G)$ contains all the subgroups of $G$ of finite index.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
We have to prove that $S(G) = \cap_{N \lhd_f G} F_N(G)$.
	Let $x \in S(G)$ and $N \lhd_f G$.
	From Lemma \ref{lemReductionRF} and Proposition \ref{propFitting} we have $Nx \in S(G/N)=F(G/N)$, i.e. $x \in F_N(G)$.\\
	On the other hand, let $x \in \cap_{N \lhd_f G} F_N(G)$ and $H \leqslant_f G$.
	If $N \lhd_f G$ is the normal core of $H$, then in particular $x \in F_N(G)$.
	From Proposition \ref{propFitting} we have
	$$ Nx \in \frac{F_N(G)}{N} = F(G/N) = S(G/N) , $$
	and so Lemma \ref{lemReductionRF} provides $x^{|G:H|} \in H$.
	The proof follows because $H$ is arbitrary.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a finite group and $N \lhd G$. Then $F(G) \leqslant F_N(G)$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
We have that $NF(G)/N \cong F(G)/(N \cap F(G))$ is a nilpotent normal subgroup of $G/N$.
	Then $NF(G)/N \leqslant F(G/N) = F_N(G)/N$, and so $NF(G) \leqslant F_N(G)$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
If $N,K \lhd_f G$ and $K \leqslant N$, then $F_K(G) \leqslant F_N(G)$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{propEquiv}
	Let $G$ be a group. The following are equivalent:
	
	\begin{itemize}
	\item[(A)] $G=S(G)$;
	\item[(B)] every subgroup of finite index of $G$ is exponential;
	\item[(C)] every finite quotient of $G$ is nilpotent;
	\item[(D)] every subgroup of finite index of $G$ is subnormal.
	\end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
This follows easily from Theorem \ref{thSExp}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a group which is residually $S$-free. Then $S(G)=1$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let $1 \neq x \in G$. By definition, there exists $N \lhd G$ such that $x \notin N$ and $S(G/N)=1$. In particular $Nx \notin S(G/N)$,
and so from Lemma \ref{lemReductionRF} we obtain $x \notin S(G)$. Since $x$ is arbitrary, it follows that $S(G)=1$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
If $F$ is a finitely generated free group, then $S(F)=1$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{propBaer}
	A group is a Baer group if and only if every its finitely generated subgroup is subnormal and nilpotent.
	In particular, every finitely generated Baer group is nilpotent.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thWilson}
	Let $G$ be a just-infinite group.
	If $B(G) \neq 1$, then $B(G)$ is a free abelian group of finite rank, which coincides with its own centralizer in $G$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a just-infinite $p$-group. Then $S(G)=G$, but $B(G)=1$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The fact that $G=S(G)$ follows from Proposition \ref{propEquiv} and the fact that finite $p$-groups are nilpotent.
	If $B(G) \neq 1$, then $B(G)$ is a free abelian group by Theorem \ref{thWilson}, which contraddicts that $G$ is a $p$-group.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{exBad}
	Let $G$ be a just-infinite $p$-group, and let $K \leqslant G$ be any nilpotent subgroup.
	Since every subgroup of finite index of $G$ is subnormal,
	from Theorem \ref{thSubn2} we have that $|HK:H|$ divides $|G:H|$ for every $H \leqslant_f G$.
	On the other hand, $K$ is not subnormal in $G$, because $B(G)=1$.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thRobinson}
	Let $G$ be a finitely generated hyperabelian or hyperfinite group. If $G$ is an $S$-group, then $G$ is nilpotent.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
